name: libxml2
workload: SAX/stream parse of in-memory synthetic XML files (wide/shallow and deep/narrow shapes averaged) at 1KB to 100MB plus real-world extracts, with empty start-element, end-element and character-data callbacks, in a Docker container per library.
claimed_speedup: SAX/Stream parse time (ms, lower is better), libxml2 vs Expat: 100KB 0.431 vs 4.59; 1MB 4.975 vs 39.008 (7.8x, derived from page data); 10MB 18.833 vs 69.255 (3.7x, derived from page data); 100MB 167.821 vs 431.529 (2.6x, derived from page data); 'other' group (unsized real-world extracts) 36.889 vs 77.918 (2.1x, derived from page data); 1KB 0.007 vs 0.010.
compiler_and_flags: Bench harness built with g++ and CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (C++17) inside debian:bookworm-slim; libxml2 and Expat are Debian bookworm apt packages (libxml2-dev, libexpat1-dev), so library build flags and versions are not pinned or stated. Benchmark source: benchmarks/libxml2/bench.cpp and benchmarks/expat/bench.cpp in https://github.com/bemayer/xml-benchmark.
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest shared runner (CPU model not stated); report generated 2026-10-01.
tradeoffs: Much larger API surface and dependency than Expat (DOM, XPath, schemas, HTML, catalogs). The repo README says it is volunteer-maintained and advises against using it on untrusted data. The harness uses the older SAX1 callback fields (startElement), not the SAX2 interface.
caveats: Third-party hobby suite (1 star, 32 commits), run on a shared CI runner with no CPU model; numbers are a monthly snapshot that changes with each run. Read from the gh-pages index.html on raw.githubusercontent.com (the live github.io page is blocked here). The report averages wide and deep shapes per size, recomputes throughput from averaged sizes, and its throughput_mbs fields are inconsistent (libxml2 1MB shows 4913 MB/s), so only time_ms is quoted. Expat times are non-monotonic (100KB 4.59 ms vs 10MB 69 ms), which suggests the deep/narrow files or per-parse overhead dominate the small sizes. The libxml2 harness passes a zeroed xmlSAXHandler with only startElement, endElement and characters set (SAX1 mode, no default SAX2 tree-building callbacks, no entity or namespace work); the Expat harness creates and frees a parser per iteration; both discard the data. A 2.1x to 7.8x SAX gap in favour of libxml2 is far larger than older reports and was not cross-checked by running it. Conflicting snippet-only evidence from search results (mail.gnome.org, python.org expat-discuss, OSM dev list and PHP docs were blocked and not opened): one developer reported libxml2 about 30% faster than Expat, another reported Expat about 10% faster on OSM files, and PHP docs call libxml2 'slightly slower for SAX'. A different harness (libsimdxml README, 1MB file, 2013 Haswell laptop) measured Expat SAX 15.5 ms against libxml2 DOM 35.2 ms, which is not a SAX-to-SAX comparison.

name: Magic Enum
baseline: conjure_enum (fix8mt/conjure_enum), another macro-free C++ enum-reflection library
workload: Compile time of translation units reflecting 200 small enums (16 members, range -128..128), 32 big enums (200 members, range -256..256) and 100 enums with an ideal range (0..50), each averaged over 10 runs, plus object-file size on Clang.
claimed_speedup: Compile time in seconds (lower is better), magic_enum vs conjure_enum: GCC Small 47 vs 97.1 (2.1x, derived from page data), Big 21 vs 81.7 (3.9x), Ideal 8.1 vs 46.8 (5.8x); Clang Small 47 vs 66.8 (1.4x), Big 18 vs 52.9 (2.9x), Ideal 8.7 vs 32 (3.7x); MSVC Big 37 vs 244.9 (6.6x), Ideal 17.9 vs 95.7 (5.3x), Small 80 vs ERROR (conjure_enum out of heap space). Clang object size KB: Small 732 vs 779, Big 1307 vs 1400, Ideal 1051 vs 1123. The Large Range case (-1024..1024) timed out (>20 min) for magic_enum on GCC and MSVC.
compiler_and_flags: -O3 for GCC and Clang, /Ox for MSVC; compiler versions not stated; conjure_enum built with FIX8_CONJURE_ENUM_MINIMAL; magic_enum range set through MAGIC_ENUM_RANGE_MAX. Generator script: benchmarks/gen.py in ZXShady/enchantum.
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 (GCC 9+, Clang 5+, MSVC 15.3+). Uses __PRETTY_FUNCTION__ probing over a bounded value range (MAGIC_ENUM_RANGE_MIN/MAX, default -128..128), so enums with larger values need per-enum customization; compile time grows with the range. Not a runtime-speed claim.
caveats: The only numbers found are in a competitor's README (enchantum). Its purpose is to show enchantum beats magic_enum: enchantum compiles 2.7x to 8.1x faster than magic_enum in the same table (for example GCC Small 6.0 s vs 47 s), simple_enum compiles faster than magic_enum in every row (GCC Small 21.5 s vs 47 s), and magic_enum's own object and executable sizes are 2.4x to 15.6x larger than enchantum's. The win over conjure_enum is implicit (the README lists conjure_enum as slow to compile with bigger binaries), conjure_enum is a niche baseline, and magic_enum is better read as the incumbent that others beat. Neither compiler versions nor CPU are stated, so this is first-party-to-a-rival, tier C. No runtime benchmark exists for magic_enum against std::string_view tables, switch statements or hand-written conversions: the repo has no benchmark directory, issue #40 has no numbers, and the Boost list thread and dev.to post that might have numbers are blocked here. Magic Enum's own README claims no speed numbers.

name: LibYAML
workload: Parse of a small CI file (travis.yml, about 4 KB) into an in-memory tree, comparing libyaml events fed into a rapidyaml tree (LibyamlParser) with YAML::Load into a yaml-cpp Node; also compile_commands.json parsed as YAML.
claimed_speedup: travis.yml parse: libyaml_arena 86.79 MB/s vs yamlcpp_arena 11.71 MB/s, shown as 7.41x on the page, CPU time per parse 0.05 ms vs 0.35 ms; compile_commands.json parse (rapidyaml README table): libyaml_arena 135.06 MB/s vs yamlcpp_arena 22.53 MB/s, 6.00x.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the result files (Google Benchmark v1.9.5, library_build_type release); benchmark source bm/bm_parse.cpp in https://github.com/biojppm/rapidyaml.
hardware: 20 logical CPUs at 4279 MHz (model name not stated), CPU scaling and ASLR disabled, Linux, run dated 2026-07-07 (results dir 0.16.0-pre).
tradeoffs: Plain C89 event-based API (no DOM), YAML 1.1 only, so a tree or typed access has to be built on top; recent releases added nest-depth limits. yaml-cpp gives a ready Node DOM and targets YAML 1.2 features.
caveats: Independent of both libraries but not a libyaml-focused suite: the rapidyaml benchmark exists to show ryml is about 3.6x faster than libyaml on this file (about 310 MB/s vs 86.79 MB/s). libyaml here is driven through rapidyaml's own test adapter that builds a ryml Tree, whereas yaml-cpp builds its own Node DOM, so the output structures differ. Compiler and flags are not in the result files and the CPU model is not named, which keeps it below tier A. Single small file for the headline row (the README adds a scatter plot over many files whose raw table was not read). yaml-cpp is a widely known slow baseline.

name: libYAML (as PyYAML CSafeLoader backend)
workload: Loading job-template YAML documents of 987 to 192,387 characters with yaml.CSafeLoader (LibYAML C parser) against yaml.SafeLoader (pure Python), in a Python project's pull request.
claimed_speedup: SafeLoader vs CSafeLoader load time: Small (987 chars) 2.91 ms vs 0.27 ms (11.0x); Large (44,187 chars) 125.74 ms vs 13.44 ms (9.4x); Extra Large (192,387 chars) 590.07 ms vs 65.48 ms (9.0x); file-based (27,347 chars) 77.26 ms vs 8.08 ms (9.6x).
tradeoffs: Needs the libyaml shared library and PyYAML built with its C extension (not always present in wheels or minimal images); YAML 1.1 semantics only; the Python object construction layer is still Python.
caveats: A PR description (merged 2025-07-31) with timings and no benchmark script, Python version, hardware or libyaml version, so tier C. The baseline is PyYAML's pure-Python loader, not a C++ library, and CSafeLoader speedup includes the Cython/C glue and the C parser together, so it is not a pure libyaml-versus-Python-parser ratio. Same repo as the 'LibYAML' record (yaml/libyaml). The pyyaml.org LibYAML wiki page was blocked and not opened; a search snippet from another source puts the C loader at about 30% faster in some cases, which conflicts with the 9x to 11x here.
